newsitem.title: USA: New wheat erodes corn demand in U.S. southeast.
newsitem.headline: New wheat erodes corn demand in U.S. southeast.

text.p: New crop soft red winter wheat is eroding some demand for corn from hog and poultry producers in the southeastern United States, cash sources said.
"When it's (wheat) available, feed mills that are grinding for their own birds become a grinder of local wheat," said one Kentucky grain dealer.
As a result of the increased demand for wheat, rail corn basis bids have softened since last week, merchandisers said.
Basis for corn at Columbus, Ohio has dropped six cents per bushel since Friday and was quoted at 24 cents per bushel over CBOT September corn futures Tuesday, cash sources said.
Demand for new crop feed wheat is particularly strong in the North Carolina and Virginia markets, where large numbers of hogs and turkeys are produced, a rail corn dealer said.
"It's a replacement feed for the hog and turkey people," the dealer said. "Corn basis would be a lot higher if the demand for corn was there."
Much of the Southeast's winter wheat crop is harvested in June, but livestock producers are still working through supplies bought when the wheat market was near harvest lows, dealers said.
"There's a feed mill in North Carolina that bought four million bushels of wheat," said one corn dealer. "North Carolina will probably use eight, maybe 10 million bushels this year."
But this week's rally in wheat prices has caused the September corn/wheat spread to widen significantly, which leaves additional wheat purchases from livestock producers unlikely, dealers said.
On Wednesday, the spread between September wheat and corn closed at $1.09 per bushel.
"The cheap wheat came in August and now wheat basis has really jumped," one merchandiser said. "They've got wheat in their bins, though, and they'll use it through August."
Livestock dealers will most likely switch back to feeding corn in September when new crop supplies in the Southeast first become available, dealers said.
